title: Beneficence and Nonmaleficence

sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Two different promises sit at the center of clinical care. One is "I will act to make you better." The other is "I will not injure you, and I will not gamble with you for no reason." Nonmaleficence is the second promise, and notice that it covers risk, not just actual damage. A nurse who gives a drug without checking the allergy list has breached it even if nothing bad happens, because the patient was put in danger that no expected benefit justified. That is why the principle is the floor everything else is built on.

### Question 2

Read the phrase carefully: it says "first," not "only." It is a rule about sequence, not a ban on action. Before you ask whether an intervention will help, you ask what it could cost the patient and whether that cost is defensible. It also does not license paralysis, because withholding needed care is itself a way of harming someone. The instruction is to make harm the first item you evaluate in every plan, every time, and to keep evaluating it as the plan changes.

### Question 3

Sort clinical actions by what would happen if the nurse did nothing. If the answer is "something bad occurs," the action was preventing harm. If the answer is "nothing bad occurs, the patient just stays where he was," the action was adding benefit. Nobody is in danger the moment a glucose meter lesson begins; the patient simply ends up more capable than he started. That forward push toward a better state, not a rescue from a worse one, is what beneficence names.

### Question 4

Compare two household rules: "cook dinner" and "do not set the kitchen on fire." The second is owed at every moment and to everyone, and you can satisfy it while asleep. The first takes effort, resources, and judgment about when and for whom, so it necessarily has limits. That asymmetry explains why the duty not to harm usually carries more weight in a conflict. It does not make beneficence optional, but it does mean a plan that helps somewhat while injuring seriously is normally rejected.

### Question 5

Two maps of the same city can draw the district lines differently without disagreeing about where the streets are. The four-principles model draws "do good" and "do no harm" as two neighboring districts. Belmont draws one district called beneficence containing both instructions. Nothing about the underlying obligation changed. The practical lesson is to read what a framework says rather than counting its headings, because the same duty can appear under different labels depending on who is drawing the map.

### Question 6

Intent is doing real work in this reasoning, and it is testable. Ask what the team would do if the pain resolved at a lower dose. If they would stop climbing, the target was the pain. If they would keep climbing anyway, the target was the sedation, and double effect no longer applies. That is also why the harmful effect cannot be the mechanism of the good: relief has to come from the analgesia itself, not from the patient being obtunded. Titration, documentation, and monitoring are what turn that claim about intent into something a reviewer can verify.

### Question 7

Beneficence has no built-in stopping point, because "for your own good" can justify nearly anything once the clinician alone defines the good. Picture a team that cancels a frail patient's weekend discharge pass to keep him safe, never learning the pass was for his daughter's wedding. The motive is sincere and the safety reasoning is real, yet the patient's own ranking of risks never entered the decision. The correction is not to care less; it is to treat "what counts as better off" as a question only this patient can finally answer.

### Question 8

Signage asking staff to be careful competes with fatigue, interruptions, and short staffing, and fatigue usually wins. A forcing function does not compete with anything: the scanner will not confirm a drug that does not match the order, so the error is stopped rather than merely discouraged. The independent double check works the same way, but only if the second nurse verifies from the original order without being told what to expect. Note the selectivity too, since requiring double checks on everything trains people to sign off reflexively, which converts a barrier into paperwork.

### Question 9

A driver can injure a pedestrian by steering into the crosswalk or by never touching the brake, and the law and ethics both count the second one. Nonmaleficence follows the same logic: what matters is whether the patient ended up harmed by something under your control, not whether your hands were moving. Immobile skin under constant pressure is on a clock, and letting that clock run is a choice with a predictable result. So the question to ask on any shift is not only "did I do anything dangerous?" but "did I leave anything undone that would predictably hurt this patient?"

### Question 10

Every safety measure has a price, and the ethical work is comparing prices rather than picking whatever stops the immediate danger. Restraints do prevent a patient from climbing out of bed, but they buy that with lost muscle, worsening confusion, skin breakdown, and occasionally severe injury when a restrained person struggles free. Nightly sedation is the same trade wearing different packaging, since it raises the very fall risk it was meant to lower. So you start with the measures whose cost is near zero, escalate only if they genuinely fail, and remember that inaction is not the neutral option, because the fall you did not try to prevent is also on your ledger.

### Question 11

Benefit and risk arrive attached to each other, which is why a package insert lists indications and adverse effects on the same page. That makes "will this help?" an incomplete question; the usable question is "does the expected help outweigh the foreseeable harm for this person?" And the answer is patient-specific, since the same anticoagulant can be clearly right for one patient and clearly wrong for another with an unstable gait and a history of bleeding. Doing good and avoiding harm are not two boxes to tick in sequence; they are one judgment made on a scale.

### Question 12

Ethics and civil law overlap but are not the same instrument, and they have different entry requirements. Negligence is a finding in a civil suit, and it does not exist without proof of all four elements, including actual damages, so a dangerous error caught before it reaches the patient produces no negligence claim at all. The ethical duty is already engaged at that point, because the patient was exposed to unjustified risk. That gap is the whole point: the law sets a floor for liability, while nonmaleficence sets a standard you are answerable to even when no one was hurt and no one sues.
